opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that drug discovery today is still mostly a trial-and-error process. We spend enormous amounts of time and money making molecules, testing them in cells and animals, and then watching roughly 90% of them fail in the clinic. So the question for predictive models isn't really "can we make one step faster," it's "can we change where the failures happen." Can we move failure earlier, into silicon, where it's cheap, instead of discovering it in a Phase II trial years and hundreds of millions of dollars later?

There are a few layers to that. The first, and the one people talk about most, is the molecular layer: predicting structure, binding, designing proteins or small molecules against a target. That's gotten dramatically better, and it's real. But I'd argue it isn't actually the main bottleneck. We're pretty good at hitting targets now. The harder problem is knowing which target to hit and what will happen to a whole cell, a whole tissue, or a whole person when you hit it.

That's where I get really excited about what you might call virtual cell models: models trained on large-scale perturbation data, like single-cell readouts from CRISPR screens and drug treatments, that learn how cells respond when you change them. If you can predict "if I knock down this gene, or add this compound, the cell moves from a disease state toward a healthy state," you're no longer just screening blindly. You're searching a space with a map. That lets you prioritize targets, find combinations, and anticipate toxicity before you ever run the experiment.

The key is that this has to be a loop, not a one-shot prediction. The model proposes experiments, the lab runs them at scale, and the results feed back to make the model better. Biology is unusual in that we can generate very high-quality, causal data with modern tools like CRISPR and single-cell sequencing. So the labs that tightly couple wet-lab experimentation with machine learning, the "lab in the loop" approach, are the ones that I think will actually compound their advantage.

And I'd be careful not to overpromise. These models won't replace clinical trials anytime soon, and biology has a long tail of complexity that will humble anyone. But if predictive models can raise the probability of success even modestly, say from 10% to 20%, that roughly halves the cost of each approved drug. That's a transformative change for patients and for the whole economics of the industry.

r001.rationale: The response ties the impact of predictive models to how much they improve success probabilities, giving a modest increase from 10% to 20% as an example of a transformative effect.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll start with the way most drugs die today, because that's where I think predictive models matter most.

The dirty secret of drug discovery is that most of the cost isn't in finding a molecule that hits a target. It's in finding out, years and hundreds of millions of dollars later, that you picked the wrong target, or that the molecule does something in a human body that nothing in your mouse or your dish told you about. Something like ninety percent of programs fail in the clinic, and the majority of those fail for efficacy, not safety. That's a prediction problem. We're running enormously expensive experiments on people to learn things we should have been able to anticipate.

So the first place I think predictive models help is in target selection and biology, not chemistry. If you can build a model of a cell that lets you ask "what happens if I knock this gene down in this cell type, in this disease context," and get an answer that's right more often than a grad student's intuition, you've changed the economics of the whole pipeline. That's what we've been trying to do at Arc with the virtual cell work. You train on massive perturbation datasets, CRISPR screens across many cell types, single-cell readouts, and you learn a model that generalizes to perturbations it hasn't seen. The goal isn't to replace the experiment. It's to run ten thousand experiments in silico so you can decide which fifty are actually worth doing at the bench.

The second place is the obvious one, which is molecular design. Protein structure prediction got solved well enough that people stopped talking about it, and now the interesting work is in generating things, not predicting them. Antibodies, enzymes, gene editors with properties nature never had a reason to evolve. We've been doing this with CRISPR systems, where you can train a language model on millions of natural sequences and sample new editors that are functional but very far from anything in the database. That was hard to imagine a few years ago.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking the models are the bottleneck. They're not. The bottleneck is data, and specifically data that's generated to train models rather than to answer one scientist's question. Most biological data is bespoke and non-comparable. If you want a foundation model for cells, you have to build the lab around producing the training set, with consistent protocols at a scale that a normal academic lab would never justify. That's an institutional problem as much as a technical one, and it's a big part of why we set Arc up the way we did.

And then the honest part: the loop has to close. A model that makes a prediction nobody tests is a paper, not a drug. The exciting version of this is a lab where the model proposes, the automation executes, the result goes back into the model, and that cycle runs in days instead of years. We're early on that. But I think that's where the real acceleration comes from, not from any single model being clever.

r001.rationale: The response links stronger predictive accuracy—getting answers right more often and generalizing to unseen perturbations—to greater impact on drug discovery economics and experiment selection.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to make the cycle between prediction and experiment much more efficient. In drug discovery, you’re searching an enormous space of possible molecules and biological interventions, and you can only test a tiny fraction of them. A useful predictive model helps you decide what to test next.

That could mean predicting whether a molecule binds to a target, but binding is only one piece of the problem. Does it produce the effect you want in a cell? Does that effect hold up across different biological contexts? Can you get it to the right tissue without causing toxicity? The closer our models get to predicting those outcomes together, the more useful they become for discovering medicines.

The key is connecting those models to experiments. You make a prediction, test it, and use the result to improve the next prediction. You also want the model to recognize where it’s uncertain, because sometimes the most valuable experiment is the one that teaches you something new. That feedback loop could help us find promising drugs faster while spending less time pursuing ideas that won’t work.

r001.rationale: The response says models become more useful for drug discovery as they get better at predicting relevant outcomes, linking predictive capability to the scale of their contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big opportunity is to make the experimental loop much more efficient. In drug discovery, you’re searching an enormous space of possible molecules, and you can only test a tiny fraction of them. A good predictive model can help you decide which experiments are most informative and which candidates are most likely to work.

But it’s not just predicting whether a molecule binds a target. You’d like to predict what happens when you perturb a biological system: Does the cell move toward a healthier state? What other pathways are affected? Could there be toxicity? Those are much harder questions, and they require richer experimental data.

So I’m excited about a loop where models propose hypotheses, experiments test them, and the results improve the models. The goal is to learn more from every experiment and increase the odds that the drugs we advance actually help patients.

r001.rationale: The response says a good predictive model can improve experiment selection and drug discovery outcomes, but it does not state that the size of capability advances depends on the model’s predictive power.
